title: Two Cave Inscriptions at Siyamangalam
html:
TWO CAVE INSCRIPTIONS AT SIYAMANGALAM.

BY E. HULTZSCH, PH.D.

The village of Śiyamaṅgalam near Dêsûr in the Wandiwash (Vandavâśi) tâluka of the North Arcot district contains a Śiva temple named Stambhêsvara or (in Tami!) Tâṇ-Āṇdâr,9 which consists of a rock-cut shrine, two maṇḍapas in front of it, and a stone enclosure.10 The two rock-cut pillars of the gate by which the shrine is entered bear the two subjoined inscriptions. Besides, there are several Chôla inscriptions on the walls of the enclosure and on the rock in the north-east corner of the temple, from which we learn that Śīyamaṅgalam belonged to Teṇṇārrūr-nādu,11 a subdivision of Palaguṇra-kōṭtam,12 a district of Jayaṅgoṇda-Chōla-maṇdalam. The temple itself was then called Tirukkarṇrali, i.e. 'the sacred stone temple' (Nos. 60 and 69 of 1900), and Tūṇ-Āṇdār (Nos. 61, 62, 63 and 65 of 1900).

A.—Inscription of Lalitānkura.

This inscription (No. 67 of 1900) is engraved on the right pillar of the gate. It consists of a single Sanskrīt verse in the Āryâ metre and is written in the same archaic alphabet as the cave inscriptions at Trichinopoly13 and Mahèndravâđi.14 It records that "this (temple) named Avanibhâjana-Pallavêsvara" was caused to be made by king Lalitānkura. From the cave inscription at Vallam15 we know that Lalitānkura was a surname of Mahèndrapôtarâja, who, according to Mr. Venkayya's researches,16 is probably identical with the Pallava king Mahèndravarman I. Two other surnames of the same king were Śatrumalla and Guṇabhara, of which the first occurs at Trichinopoly and Vallam, and the second at Trichinopoly, Vallam and Mahèndravâđi. Thus the Pallava king Mahèndravarman I., who reigned about the beginning of the seventh century of the Christian era, is now known to have excavated four rock-cut shrines, of which that at Mahèndravâđi was dedicated to Vishṇu, and the three others to Śīva. The name of the Śīyamaṅgalam cave, Avanibhâjana-Pallavêsvara, means 'the Āsvara (i.e. Śīva temple) of the Pallava (king) Avanibhâjana.' Hence Avanibhâjana,17 i.e. 'the possessor of the earth,' must have been another surname of Mahèndravarman I.

  2. 2 nibhâja[na]-Pallavêsvaran=nâma [|*]
  3. 3 kâritam=êtat=svê[dh]â(chchhâ)-karaṇda-
  4. 4 m=iva puṇya-ratnânâm [||*]

TRANSLATION.

By king Lalitānkura was caused to be made this (temple) named Avanibhâjana-Pallavêsvara—a casket, as it were, (worked at) his will (and enclosing) jewels, (viz.) good deeds.19

B.—Inscription of Vijaya-Nandivikramavarman.

This inscription (No. 68 of 1900) is engraved on the left pillar of the gate. Its alphabet is Tamiļ, with the exception of the Grantha words svasti śrī at the beginning and śrī in line 10, and resembles that of the Tiruvallam rock inscription of Vijaya-Nandivikramavarman; but the letter ṇ has throughout its archaic form, while in the Tiruvallam inscription the modern form with fully developed central loop occurs twice.20—The language is Tamiļ. As in the Madras Museum plates of Jaṭilavarman,21 the rules of saṅdhi are not observed in Perumbálaiúr (l. 7 f.) for Perumbálaiyúr and in aliámai (l. 14) for aliýamai, which is an archaic form of the negative gerund aliýamal. The final n of kiļavaņ (l. 9) is doubled before the following vowel. The Tamiļ form mugamanđugam (l. 14) instead of the Sanskrit mukhamanđapa has been already noticed in the Ukkal inscription of Krīshpā III.22

The inscription is dated in the third year of the reign of Vijaya-Nandivikramavarman, whom I have identified with the father of the Ganga-Pallava king Vijaya-Nřipatuńgavikramavarman and placed in the ninth century of the Christian-era.23 This is the earliest known inscription of Vijaya-Nandivikramavarman. Five other records of his at Šaduppěri, Viriňchipuram and Tiruvallam are dated between his 9th and 62nd years.24 Since the publication of the two Āmbúr inscriptions of Vijaya-Nřipatuńgavikramavarman,25 two inscriptions of his grandfather Vijaya-Dantivikramavarman26 and four inscriptions of his own reign27 were copied at Uttaramallúr in the Chingleput district. The Šađaiyar temple at Tiruchecheňnambúnđi near Kôvilađi (between Tanjore and Trichinopoly) contains three inscriptions of the same king.28 Two of these mention Māřambávai, “who was the great queen of Nandippôttaraiyar of the Pallavatila[ka ?] family.”29 The same queen is referred to in an inscription at Niyamam in the Tanjore táluka (No. 16 of 1899), which is unfortunately mutilated, but seems to belong to the reign of the early Chôła king Rájakėsarivarman. One feels tempted to conclude from this that Rájakėsarivarman put an end to the rule of the Gańga-Pallavas, and that certain chiefs who claimed connection with the Pallava dynasty were first subordinate to Vijaya-Nřipatuńgavikramavarman and afterwards to his conqueror, the Chôła king.

The inscription records that the manđapa in front of the cave temple was built by a certain Ađavi with the permission of a Gańga chief named Něrguťti, who must have been subordinate to Vijaya-Nandivikramavarman. Ađavi was the headman of a village near Perumbálaiyúr in ŕřrukkáťtu-kôťtam. This district owes its name to ŕřrukkáđu, a village in the Conjeeveram táluka, and Perumbálaiyúr is perhaps the same as Pálaiyúr which is mentioned in the Kaśákúđi plates.9

TRANSLATION.

(Line 1.) Hail! Prosperity! In the third year (of the reign) of king Vijaya-Nandivikramavarman,— Ađavi, the headman of Tiruppâlaiyûr (near) Perumbâlaiyûr in Ūṛṛukkâṭtu-kôṭṭam, having made a request to (i.e. having obtained the sanction of) the glorious Gaṅga king Nêrguṭti Perumâṇ,— (this) Ađavi made the maṇdapa in front (of the shrine) for (the merit of) his mother Naṅga[ṇ]i Naṅgai.

(L. 14.) The feet of him who protects this (gift) without destroying (it), (shall be) on my head.32

Footnotes

1(p. 319, n. 1) The second singular imperative is addressed to the official at Kûdûra. The verb oyapâpeti is probably derived from avayava, the v having been hardened into p as in apâpesa (L. 31). In the Kârlê inscription No. 19 read also oyapâpehi instead of deya papahi (A. S. W. I. Vol. IV. p. 112, text line 3).

2(p. 319, n. 2) See note 1 above. I believe that the second singular imperative is also intended in A. S. W. I. Vol. IV. p. 112, text line 4 (parihariha), p. 104, text line 4, and p. 111, text line 14 (pariharîhi); and the second plural imperative ibid. p. 106, text line 11 (pariheretha).

3(p. 319, n. 3) The second singular imperative nibaṅdhâpehi, which is quite clear on the copper plate, has been misread in various ways in A. S. W. I. Vol. IV. p. 105, text line 5, p. 111, text line 14, and p. 112, text line 5. The second plural imperative (nibaṅdhâpetha) is meant ibid. p. 106, text line 11.

4(p. 319, n. 4) On aviyena see A. S. W. I. Vol. IV. p. 105, note 2.

5(p. 319, n. 5) In his valuable paper on the Kârlê inscriptions, which will appear in Vol. VII. of this journal, Dr. Senart derives chhata from kshaṇ, ‘to hurt’ and hence ‘to write.’ The king cannot have written the order himself, because the inscription expressly states that he issued it by word of mouth. Hence I propose to translate chhata by ‘signed.’ The king’s signature may have been affixed to the original document, which was deposited in the royal secretariat, and from which the copper-plates were copied. In the latter the royal signature is represented by the seal on which they are strung.

6(p. 319, n. 6) On sattâ see Ind. Ant. Vol. XIV. p. 332.

7(p. 319, n. 7) Compare the Kârlê inscription No. 19, where Dr. Senart (see note 5 above) reads vijayathasatâre or satâkhe. If the second alternative is accepted, the compound would mean “victory, wealth, power and fame.”

8(p. 319, n. 8) This passage is a kind of docket, stating the contents of the whole document.
